title: Invisible classrooms: What we’ve learned about education news since the Nikole Hannah-Jones essay
author: Isobel Stevenson
summary: Former school leader Isobel Stevenson, writing as a guest in The Grade, argues that education journalism almost never examines what happens in classrooms. She starts from the 2010 Los Angeles Times series on teacher value-added, which showed that instruction varies more within schools than between them, and notes that the finding was largely forgotten. She then uses the coverage of Nikole Hannah-Jones's New York Times Magazine essay as a test case, counting how little of the following two and a half weeks of reporting addressed instruction or learning. Her review of The Grade's own last year of stories found only about 10% substantially concerned instruction or curriculum. Even strong pieces from the New York Times default to policy-level fixes such as mayoral control and integration rather than the quality of teaching. Her conclusion is that if instruction is the core mechanism for opportunity, journalists should investigate how instructional systems work and why weak teaching is tolerated.
points: The 2010 LA Times finding that teacher quality varies more within schools than between them implies that which teacher a child gets matters more than which school, yet this insight has faded from public discussion.
Stevenson's quick audit shows that only about a tenth of roughly 240 education stories in a year dealt substantially with instruction or curriculum, and a third of those were about reading reform.
Coverage of the Hannah-Jones essay described poor teaching vividly but did not ask how it arose or why it persisted, which leaves readers without any systemic explanation.
Policy-level remedies such as mayoral control and integration dominate the news even though they sit far from students' daily experience and have a mixed record.
The practical implication for school leaders is to monitor and reduce classroom-to-classroom variation in instruction, since the press is unlikely to do it for them.
quotes: Classroom instruction is a fundamental mechanism for perpetuating or disrupting inequity. Schools and districts organize instruction — more by default than by design — so that some kids consistently get much more opportunity to learn than others.
In an 8,000-word essay about a child’s schooling, there is vivid description of poor teaching but little investigation of how it came to be and why it’s tolerated.

We have good evidence that there is more variation in the quality of instruction from class to class than from school to school — in other words, which teacher my kid gets matters more to their future outcomes than which school they go to.
The great irony here is that teaching, implemented well, would reduce the need for these interventions, but the article says almost nothing about instruction.
The coverage defaults to policy-level solutions such as mayoral control and integration, interventions that are much further from students’ experiences and have a mixed track record of success.

Why, then, are we not asking what it would take for all students to experience high quality instruction? What makes us think that we can implement interventions well, when we cannot even guarantee that all teachers teach adequately?
